editorial:
The Dragon Painter is a 1919 American silent romantic drama directed by William Worthington and produced by Sessue Hayakawa through his own Haworth Pictures Corporation, with distribution by Robertson-Cole. Hayakawa plays Tatsu, a reclusive mountain painter who believes his lost love was transformed into a dragon; location photography in Yosemite Valley and at Coronado, California's Japanese Tea Garden gives the film an expansive visual scale rare at its budget level. The Library of Congress selected it for the National Film Registry in 2014 as culturally, historically, and aesthetically significant. It is among the earliest American features with an almost entirely Asian cast, and the print layer â€” the original 1919 footage itself â€” is free to use in the United States.

The practical rights trap is the restoration layer. The 2024 Milestone Films and Kino Lorber Blu-ray presents a 2023 4K digital restoration by the San Francisco Silent Film Festival, Eye Filmmuseum, and George Eastman Museum; that presentation is a separately copyrightable work. The Blu-ray also carries two newly commissioned scores by Mas Koga and Makia Matsumura, each an independent protected recording. Copying from the Blu-ray means taking Milestone's licensed restoration version and those scores, not the bare 1919 original. The Internet Archive item (identifier: silent-the-dragon-painter) predates the 2023 restoration and is the more practicable PD source, though its provenance traces to the 1988 AFI/George Eastman House/MoMA restoration; anyone building commercial work on this footage should confirm the specific digitization's provenance before relying on it.
faq: Can I incorporate footage from The Dragon Painter in my own film or video?

The 1919 film is public domain in the United States by copyright term expiry, so using a PD source print is legally permitted. The issue is which copy you source from. The Milestone Films/Kino Lorber Blu-ray contains the 2023 4K restoration by the San Francisco Silent Film Festival, Eye Filmmuseum, and George Eastman Museum â€” that specific version carries its own copyright. Use the Internet Archive copy or another pre-restoration digitization and verify its provenance before building commercial work on it.
Is the music in available copies of The Dragon Painter free to use?

No. As a silent film, the 1919 original has no recorded score. Any musical accompaniment in a modern copy was added later and is protected separately. The Milestone/Kino Lorber Blu-ray includes two scores by Mas Koga and Makia Matsumura commissioned for the 2024 release, both under their own copyright. To use the film with free music you must either add your own, or source a copy with pre-1928 period accompaniment whose copyright status you have independently verified.
